AI Projects

Eight projects below — a rail-yard simulation, a combat AI, a doctrine-driven wargaming system, a continuous 3D garden world, two sports forecasters, an AI reading harness for historical texts, a position piece on where AI takes game design, and the tools behind them. Each write-up includes what the check found, including results that got worse. The AI-collaboration methodology is disclosed once, at the bottom of this page.

dryport — a rail yard, modeled to find what actually works flagship

A discrete-event simulation (Python/SimPy) of a rail-served container yard, replayed live in 3D (Three.js). The starting question was concrete: when you can't know exactly when a container will leave — only a coarse signal about which group it's in — which stacking policy and yard-management approach actually cuts wasted crane moves? Answering it meant building several candidate policies and testing them against each other under identical, repeated conditions.

What actually works, discovered by testing it:

  • The best policy works from a deliberately imprecise estimate of when each container will leave, since no yard has perfect institutional memory — and it nearly halves rehandles against no policy at all (1.474 → 0.765), with the advantage holding up even as that estimate gets noisier.
  • Two intuitively "smarter" ideas made things worse. Matching trains to yard tracks by cargo composition was actively harmful — it broke a load-balancing effect the simplest baseline had been providing by accident. Aiming the crane's idle time at the single most-overdue container backfired the same way: most of those moves chased a container whose predicted pickup time had already passed, one box alone absorbing a fifth of all idle-time work in a single run.

What checking the model's own assumptions turned up — an equally useful result:

  • Ran a systematic audit of all 57 constants in the simulation against industry data (BLS wage data, EPRI equipment studies, PierPASS terminal statistics, federal rail regulation). Found six calibration errors of 2×–99× — including a crane-speed figure that had confused two physically different machines, corrected against the manufacturer's own technical document.
  • Retested every published finding that depended on the corrected constants. Two changed. One algorithm's "harmful" verdict disappeared once the trains were sized correctly. A stacking strategy shown winning "at every noise level" turned out to lose at the noisiest end once retested.
  • The 3D replay viewer caught what the summary numbers couldn't. A dedicated check against the simulation's own event log — the same log the viewer renders from — found a bay silently stacked 188 boxes high against a 5-tier physical limit. Every KPI the project tracked looked normal; nothing about it was visible until something had to draw it.
  • A stacking-priority rule in the project's own design document read as plausible and was, in fact, backwards. Built and measured as a control, it scored worse than having no policy at all, on every seed tested.

The corrections sit next to the original numbers in the project's own changelog.

gladiator-arena — a working viewer turned out to be a working bug detector public repo

A combat simulator built on D&D 5e-style mechanics: four classes and six races, each with its own stat modifiers, a d20 roll against Armor Class for every attack, a critical hit on a natural 20, and named class abilities — fireball, sneak attack, sacred flame, second wind — each resolved with its own damage dice. Line-of-sight, per-class movement AI, and personality traits drive how each unit actually plays those rules out, paired with a live 3D viewer built the same session. Two Clerics locked twelve tiles apart within minutes of the first watch, and that one frozen match opened into two separate discoveries: what each class's AI should actually do, and what a purely numeric view of 5,246 archived matches had been hiding the whole time.

What sensible AI behavior turned out to require:

  • Cleric had exactly two behaviors — heal a wounded ally, or flee a nearby threat — and nothing else. With neither condition met, it did nothing, forever. Fixed by adding a third branch: close distance and fight, the same baseline every other class already had.
  • Rogue's sneak-attack bonus fired on every attack regardless of whether its own flanking movement had succeeded, making that AI decorative. Fixed to require the position it was already supposed to be checking for.
  • Rogue (and any sufficiently cowardly Fighter) stopped one tile short of its own attack range on approach — an off-by-one that fired on nearly every attempt. Averaged 0.05–0.17 kills/match against 0.40–0.85+ for every other class, never flagged anywhere in the project's history until this pass. Fixed and re-verified at 0.28–0.55.

What a purely numeric view had been hiding:

  • The bug behind the frozen match had been live for the project's whole history — the old 2D viewer and 5,246 archived matches never surfaced it. The 3D viewer did, within minutes of the first watch.
  • Every stalemate timeout had been silently recorded as a decisive win — 408 of 408 cases, 7.8% of the whole archive — because the result-builder checked only whether one team was still standing, with no separate draw case. Those phantom wins had also been quietly feeding a unit's "bravery" trait, which itself gated the cowardly-Fighter version of the off-by-one above.

The 408 already-misrecorded matches stay in the archive unedited — fixing the code and documenting what happened mattered more than rewriting old scores. Character assets are CC0, sourced by driving itch.io's interactive download flow through headless Chrome end to end, since there was no plain download URL to fetch.

AI wargaming — where the chess pieces talk back public repo

Named subordinate officers aren't stat blocks here — their personality is load-bearing. Established once, it survives across sessions correctly, and it actively predicts and constrains what an officer will do, the way managing a subordinate does. That pairs with the other half of the same body of work: EPOCH, a coded combat engine that tests doctrine claims empirically.

  • A subordinate's personality becomes a tactical risk the player has to manage. Cmdr Sorn was established once as "aggressive, effective." Months later, facing an unknown invasion force, the campaign doesn't just reuse the label — it predicts off it: Sorn will want to fight straight, and that will get him killed if the player lets it go that far. The officer's history is doing the work here.
  • Officers stay themselves in ways that pay off later. Cmdr Pelleen ("distant but loyal") went dark investigating a signal on his own initiative — consistent with "distant," and the one who actually finds the threat, which is what "loyal" turns out to mean. Lt Cmdr Veris (Intelligence) is reliably the officer who figures it out first, every time he shows up.
  • The same design survives a jump to a completely different rule system. In a BattleTech campaign, a Clan officer stays honor-bound to a single named target under Zellbrigen — a documented canonical mechanic — until the code breaks, at which point her own tactical behavior changes, from disciplined single combat to an open brawl.
  • The other half is measured directly. A 130-battle tournament across 11 theaters (EPOCH) put doctrine claims to the test directly: Passive beat Aggressive by 78 Elo points (1039 vs. 961), every decisive engagement — 10 of 10 — going to the more disciplined side. The same three archetypes get reused under different names depending on the ruleset running — screen-and-commit, mass-assault, feint-and-flank — with no shared code between them.

The Estate — an AI Garden Experience complete

A continuous Three.js world: garden sections built one at a time around a Japanese/zen core, the same way a botanical garden grows over years. For when you want to build, and walk through, your own relaxing place of beauty.

  • Seven sections built in sequence inside one continuous scene: a Japanese/zen core (pond, moon bridge, a monk who rakes the sand court on a timer), a European hedge-and-parterre frame, a Rose Garden, a Vineyard, a Desert Garden modeled on the Huntington's own, a Stand of Trees — an 18th-century English "wilderness" grove, 21 distinct tree species along a winding path to a hidden obelisk clearing — and a Garden House.
  • The Garden House is a teahouse, modeled on the Huntington's own ceremonial teahouse Seifu-an, approached by a roji of stepping stones past a tsukubai wash basin. It's the one building anywhere in the Estate, by deliberate exception — everything else is outdoor planting and landscaping.
  • 44,704 instanced objects in the Rose Garden alone (twelve documented rose-color classes, spread across every bed), 33,885 in the Vineyard (six wine-grape varieties across twelve blocks).
  • The zen court's raking patterns now cycle randomly through the named traditional designs (concentric ripples, waves, ichimatsu), replacing the previous fixed rotation.

Sports forecasting — 12,039 predictions, every one logged public repo

An Elo-rating forecaster for MLB and NBA, built to answer the same kind of question as dryport in a different domain: which approach predicts better once it's checked against outcomes it never got to peek at. Every prediction is walk-forward — backfilled using only data that would have been available before that game — and logged whether it hits or misses.

The discipline behind the numbers:

  • The model's assumptions are all named up front: a K-factor of 20, home-court worth 65 rating points, and a third of every team's rating pulled back toward the mean each season.
  • MLB clears the -110 betting break-even line (52.38%) by about 2.5 points — a small, marginal edge, and the write-up says so plainly.
  • NBA clears the same line by roughly 12 points, comfortably. All 12,039 predictions behind these numbers, including every miss, sit in an open accuracy ledger — nothing curated out after the fact.

ltui — an AI discussion harness for historical and traditional texts private — architecture only

A terminal reading station that normalizes 60 differently-shaped corpora of historical, traditional, and cultural texts into one browsable schema, then pairs the reader with a local model that streams its response token-by-token inside the same interface — the model's thinking stays visible while browsing keeps going.

  • A per-source adapter layer maps each corpus's own field names onto one shared passage schema (header, text, attribution, translation, tags) before the reader ever sees it, so a new source plugs in as a single adapter function.
  • The inference panel runs as an async worker inside the TUI and updates as tokens arrive, keeping a passage on screen and searchable while the model's response streams beside it.
  • Two perspective-taking response modes — a single discussion and a multi-voice duet — sit behind the same keypress used to read a passage plainly, keeping the model's take one key away.
  • A study workflow collects multiple passages, sends them to the model as one prompt asking what they hold in common, and exports the result for further work.

The corpora themselves stay private — a mixture of historical, traditional, and cultural source material. What's shown here is the harness built around them: source-agnostic normalization paired with a live, streaming reading panel.

The future of gaming — a fixed world loses to a live one position piece

The claim: a fixed, pre-authored game world — even one as sophisticated as GTA6 — becomes a worse entertainment product than a live, continuously AI-customized alternative on the same hardware class, as AI compute keeps getting cheaper. The traditional engine doesn't break. The comparison it's judged against moves, and a fixed product can't move with it.

Current evidence for this claim, dated and cited:

  • Google DeepMind's Genie 3 already generates an explorable 3D world from a text prompt, navigable live, and lets a player inject changes mid-session — add an element, shift the weather, reshape the environment — through the same interface used to move around in it. Publicly demoable since January 2026.
  • GameNGen and Oasis go further in a narrower case: both run existing games (DOOM, Minecraft) with no traditional engine underneath — a neural model predicts every frame directly from player input, frame by frame.
  • On the NPC side, Inworld AI and NVIDIA ACE are shipping LLM-driven characters with persistent memory into production Unreal/Unity pipelines today, and a 2026 industry survey puts NPC-AI adoption at 54% of studios.

The honest counter-case, kept in:

  • World models still can't do what a traditional engine does by design — track what exists. They predict the next frame; they lack a persistent, queryable game state the way a rules-and-physics engine maintains one. Inference carries a per-frame cost a traditional renderer doesn't pay.
  • The dominant informed industry prediction right now is a hybrid: a world-model layer running inside or alongside a conventional engine, still standing, still doing the work only it can do. That's the sharper version of the claim above, and a stronger one: the fixed thing stops being the best use of a given compute budget once live, per-player customization keeps getting cheaper to run — the engine stays, the case for shipping a fixed world on top of it weakens every year.

Three systems already built, offered here as evidence:

  • playset, open-sourced the same night as this piece, is the most direct evidence of the mechanism above, running: a small three.js renderer plus a versioned JSON contract where a deterministic engine owns all state and an AI only narrates on top of it — never touching the scene. Played a D&D encounter through it live, round by round, watching the 3D board update itself as the story went — a demonstration of the buildable "hybrid" version of this thesis, the trajectory the honest counter-case above already predicts.
  • gladiator-arena's combat AI demonstrates the NPC-feedback half of this: unit personality traits (aggression, cunning, bravery) drive behavior and outcomes, verified directly against thousands of archived matches.
  • The AI wargaming doctrine project goes further — a named subordinate officer's established personality actively predicts and constrains what they'll do across sessions, and the same design survives a full genre swap, from a D&D-style campaign to BattleTech's Zellbrigen mechanic, with no shared code between the two rule systems. Most public writing on this topic argues from what might happen. These are working systems already showing a piece of it happening.

Methodology

Every project above was built collaboratively with Claude Code, and the same practice runs through all of them: build something — a simulation, a live 3D view of it, a backtest — that can disagree with an assumption, then run it and report what it says, even when that means reversing a published result. Visual, interactive models turned out to be a scalable, affordable way to do that: cheap to build, able to surface problems a spreadsheet of KPIs won't show — a bay stacked 188 boxes past its physical limit, a match that quietly never ends — and worth building again on whatever comes next.

Built and published the same evening it describes.
